To add arguments in a formal register: per giunta, peraltro, del resto, inoltre.
To express opposition: tuttavia, ciononostante, nondimeno, viceversa.

Florence, December. Pietro's school is taking part in a debate tournament between the city's schools. The topic: "Is tourism a resource or a threat for Florence?". By drawing lots, Pietro has to defend tourism. Valeria Conti is coaching him.
It's not fair. I think tourism is a threat and I have to say it's a resource.
On the contrary, it's perfect. A good speaker must know how to defend even the thesis he doesn't share.
All right. So: tourism brings jobs. And it also brings money to the museums.
Too simple. In a formal debate you don't say "and… and". You say "on top of that" or "besides".
"Tourism brings jobs; on top of that, it funds the museums." Like that?
Exactly. And when your opponent says it empties the neighbourhood?
I'll say it isn't tourism that empties it, but the lack of rules.
Very good. "But rather" after a negation. And then rephrase: "in other words, the problem isn't the tourist, that is the person, but the system".
And at the end? How do I finish?
With a formal conclusion: "Therefore, tourism is a resource, provided it is managed." It follows that you've won.
And what if the opponent is Davide? His school is in the other group.
Then, after all, the best one will win. And you both trained in this trattoria.
Stress on the last syllable: ben-SÌ.
and on top of that (an extra argument, often negative)
È caro; per giunta, è lontano.
Il dato, peraltro, è noto da anni.
Del resto, anche i turisti vogliono una città viva.
"Del resto" justifies what you said before, as an obvious argument: "Era stanco; del resto, aveva lavorato tutta la notte."
Ciononostante, molte famiglie se ne vanno.
Le case si svuotano; viceversa, gli alberghi si riempiono.
"Ciononostante" = ciò + nonostante = "in spite of this". It is a key word for essays and debates.
Non è un problema, anzi: è un’opportunità.
Non è una minaccia, bensì una risorsa.
"Bensì" appears only after a negation and is formal. In speech people say "ma": "Non è una minaccia, ma una risorsa."
Il centro, cioè le strade intorno al Duomo.
Il turismo di massa, ossia milioni di persone l’anno.
Il 60%, vale a dire più della metà.
In altre parole, il problema è il sistema.
Rephrasing is a debating weapon: you repeat the idea in other words to fix it in the jury's mind.
Pertanto, il turismo è una risorsa.
Ragion per cui chiediamo nuove regole.
In a formal speech: you open with innanzitutto, add with per giunta, oppose with ciononostante, correct with bensì, rephrase with ossia and close with pertanto.
It isn't a problem; on the contrary, it's an opportunity.
Which connector appears ONLY after a negation?
In other words, the problem is the system.

The debate tournament of Florence's middle schools was held every year in December, in the great hall of the Biblioteca delle Oblate, with windows facing the dome of the Duomo. Sixteen schools took part, divided into two groups. Each team was made up of three pupils, and each debate lasted twenty minutes: three minutes of opening for each side, two minutes of rebuttal, one of conclusion. That year the topic had been chosen by the city council: "Is tourism a resource or a threat for Florence?". And the side to defend was drawn by lot, that very morning, in front of everyone.

Pietro was the captain of his school's team, together with two classmates, Bianca and Sara. When the Italian teacher had suggested it to him, in October, he had accepted at once. After the television and the story of the T, he felt almost an expert in debates. Then, in November, the news everyone was waiting for, and that he dreaded, arrived: in the other group was the school from San Frediano, Davide's school. And Davide was the captain. "If we both reach the final," Davide had said with a smile, "I'll destroy you." "On the contrary," Pietro had replied, "I'll destroy you."

For a month, the trattoria in via Maggio became a training room again. On Mondays and Wednesdays Pietro trained, with Valeria Conti as coach. On Tuesdays and Thursdays Davide trained, with Mancini, who had volunteered "for equal opportunities". Graziella, who served dinner to both of them, had set a rule: neither of them was to listen to the other's training. But Lupino, who knew nothing about rules, went from one table to the other and, according to Pietro, played the spy.

Valeria taught Pietro the connectors of formal discourse, the ones nobody ever uses at school. "In a debate," she explained, "what matters is not only what you say, but how you link things together. A good argument without connectors is like a necklace without a string: the pearls fall on the floor." So Pietro learned to say "on top of that" instead of "and then", "nevertheless" instead of "but", "but rather" after a negation, "that is" to rephrase, "therefore" to conclude. He wrote them on coloured cards and repeated them in the shower, until his mother asked him whether he was preparing for a law exam.

Mancini, with Davide, used a different method. He didn't teach him words, but questions. "A journalist," he told him, "doesn't win because he speaks well. He wins because he finds the question the other person can't answer." So on Tuesdays and Thursdays Davide spent his evenings looking for the weak points of the opposing thesis, noting in a notebook every possible objection, even the strangest ones. Graziella, passing between the tables with the plates, sometimes stopped to listen for a few seconds, then shook her head. "These two boys," she said one evening to Bellini, "will end up as lawyers. And then there'll really be trouble." Bellini laughed. "Worse," he replied. "They'll become journalists. Lawyers at least get paid to argue."

The first round went well. The second, too. In the semi-final Pietro's team had to argue that tourism is a threat, that is the thesis he really believed in, and won easily against a school from Novoli. On the other side, Davide's team reached the final by beating the most famous art school in the city, with a speech by Davide about the murals of his neighbourhood that made a teacher on the jury cry. So, on 18 December, in the hall of the Oblate, they found themselves facing each other, as Davide had promised. And fate, that morning, decided the sides: Pietro's team would defend tourism as a resource. Davide's, as a threat.

On the morning of the final, before leaving, Pietro found Bellini sitting in the trattoria, at his usual table, with a coffee and the newspaper. He had come specially, at eight, something his cardiologist had forbidden. "Just one piece of advice," he said, without raising his eyes from the paper. "Pauses." Pietro didn't understand. "When you say something important," Bellini explained, "stop. Two seconds. Let the room feel it. Children all speak too fast, as if they were afraid of silence. But silence is your most powerful connector. It's worth more than all the 'therefores' in the world." Then he patted him on the shoulder and went back to his paper, as if he hadn't said anything important.

Pietro felt his heart sink. It was the wrong thesis, the one he didn't believe in. Davide, on the other side of the table, threw him a triumphant smile. But Valeria, sitting in the front row among the spectators, made a sign with her hand, as if to say: it's perfect. And Pietro remembered what she had told him on the first day: a good speaker must know how to defend even the thesis he doesn't share. Indeed, that one above all. Because to defend it well, you must truly understand the people who think differently.

Everyone was among the spectators. Graziella in the front row, with her coat for great occasions and a bag that, Pietro was sure, contained a thermos labelled "tea". Rita and Efisio, Davide's grandfather, with a handmade sign: "Go, San Frediano". Bellini, with his walking stick leaning against the chair. Giulia and Matei with Viola, who had brought the wooden spoon "to clap". On the jury there were three people: a university professor, a radio journalist and councillor Neri, who had promised to be impartial and who, to be sure, had not greeted either of the two boys.

Davide opened. He spoke about the murals in his neighbourhood, about the closed shops, about his mother who was paying the highest rent of her life. He spoke about his grandfather, Efisio, who came with a shovel in 1966 to save a city that now, he said, "risks becoming a museum without inhabitants". He was excellent. He used the connectors Mancini had taught him: "First of all… on top of that… it follows that…". When he finished, the audience applauded at length. Efisio raised the sign above his head. Graziella, who in theory should have been supporting Pietro, applauded louder than anyone.

Then it was Pietro's turn. He stood up, looked at the audience, looked at Davide, and decided to begin in a way nobody expected. "I agree with almost everything my opponent has said," he said. There was a murmur. Davide looked at him in surprise. "Nevertheless," Pietro went on, "I think he has picked the wrong target. Florence's problem is not tourism, but the lack of rules. In other words: it isn't the tourist who empties the neighbourhood, that is the person who comes to see the Uffizi, but a system that allows every house to be turned into a hotel."

"Tourism brings jobs," said Pietro. "On top of that, it funds the museums and the restorations. I know it well, because my family restored a Caravaggio in Malta with the money from tourists' tickets. Besides, tourists don't want an empty city. They come to Florence to eat ribollita in real trattorias, not in fake restaurants for tourists. After all, if the neighbourhood dies, tourism dies too." He paused, as Bellini had taught him. "Therefore, tourism is a resource. But, like every resource, it must be managed. It follows that we must not fight the tourists, but write better rules."

The audience stayed silent for a second, then applauded. Davide, in his rebuttal, tried to attack: he said rules weren't enough, that the money from tourism doesn't reach the families of the neighbourhood, but the owners who live in Milan. It was a good argument. Pietro knew it, because it was the same one he would have used. So, in his rebuttal, he did something Valeria hadn't taught him. He agreed with Davide. "My opponent is right," he said. "Indeed, he is more right than I am on this point. And that is exactly why we need rules: so that the money stays here. That is, in the shops, in the trattorias, in the homes of people like his mother."

Davide looked at Pietro for a long time. Then, against all the rules of the tournament, he smiled. In his conclusion he said something that wasn't written on his cards. "My opponent has just agreed with me and, at the same time, beaten me," he said. "I don't know how he did it. But I know that, if tourism is a resource, it is only if someone manages it the way he said. Therefore, I too ask for better rules. After all, I've always thought like him. We were just defending the wrong sides." The audience burst out laughing. Viola banged the wooden spoon on her chair.

The jury withdrew for ten minutes. When it returned, the university professor read the verdict. "We have witnessed a debate different from the others," she said. "Usually pupils try to destroy their opponent. Today, on the contrary, we saw two opponents who listened to each other. The jury has decided, unanimously, to award victory to Pietro's team, for the quality of the argumentation and of the connectors." There was applause. "However," the professor went on, "the jury has also decided to award a special prize, which did not exist until today, to Davide, for the most honest conclusion we have ever heard in this tournament."

Pietro and Davide went up together to collect their prizes. Pietro received a small silver cup, slightly crooked. Davide received a medal and a certificate, handwritten by councillor Neri: "For proving that, in a debate, you can also win by agreeing with the other side". Davide read it aloud, then turned to Pietro. "I told you I'd destroy you," he said. "On the contrary," Pietro replied, "we destroyed each other. It follows that we both won." Councillor Neri, who had promised to be impartial, finally hugged them both.

As the audience was leaving the hall, Lorenzo, the baker's grandson, came up to Pietro. He had come too, at the back of the hall, without telling anyone. "That thing about rules," he said, a little embarrassed. "I heard it. I rent two flats to tourists, you know. And you know what? You're right. I've just spoken to councillor Neri. The council is preparing a new regulation and is looking for owners willing to take part in the meetings." He paused. "I said yes. Not that I've become a saint. But, after all, if the neighbourhood dies, I die too." Pietro smiled. It was the first time someone had used one of his sentences against him, and he was happy.

That evening, at the trattoria, the cup and the certificate were put on the kitchen shelf, next to the tin box, the blue brush, the photos of Aldo and Viorica and Bellini's book. Graziella said the shelf was becoming a museum and that soon she would have to put a plaque there too. Efisio told everyone, for the third time, the story of the shovel of 1966. And Mancini, who had coached Davide, and Valeria, who had coached Pietro, sat down at the same table to discuss, with many connectors, which of them had been the better coach.

At about ten a message arrived on Giulia's phone. It was Professor Ruggeri, from Rome. He had seen the video of the final on the "Gazzetta" website, where Mancini had posted it right after the prize-giving. "Dear colleague," he wrote, "the boy on the scaffolding has just done in six minutes what took me thirty years to learn: to agree with your opponent without losing your thesis. Tell him that, nevertheless, I remain sceptical about the T. But that, if one day he wants to become an art historian, my door is open. Indeed, wide open." Giulia read the message aloud. Pietro said nothing, but all evening he held Giulia's phone in his hand, rereading the last word.

"Pietro won," said Valeria. "Therefore, my method was better." "Nevertheless," replied Mancini, "Davide received the special prize, which didn't exist. It follows that my method invented a new prize." "After all," said Valeria, "he got the special prize for agreeing with Pietro, that is with my pupil." "But rather," Mancini retorted, "for honesty, which can't be taught, that is it's his merit and no coach's." Bellini, from his table, rolled his eyes. "Enough," he said. "You've just shown that connectors, badly used, only serve to argue elegantly."

Later, after the guests had left, Pietro and Davide stayed sitting on the trattoria steps, in the cold, watching the Christmas lights hung between the houses of via Maggio. Davide had the certificate in his hand, Pietro the crooked cup. "You know what?" said Davide. "When you said you agreed with me, I felt disarmed. I'd prepared three attacks and didn't use any of them." Pietro laughed. "Giulia taught me," he said. "On television, against Ruggeri. You don't win by destroying the other person. You win by making them an ally."

Davide thought for a moment. Then he took a folded sheet out of his rucksack and gave it to him. It was a drawing, made that very evening, in secret, during dinner: two boys sitting opposite each other at a table, with coloured cards in their hands, and above them, instead of comic-strip speech bubbles, only two words. Above the boy with brown hair was written "on the contrary". Above the one with black hair, "but rather". "It's for your diary," said Davide. "That way, in fifty years, when someone reads it, they'll know we argued. But with the right connectors."

Pietro stuck the drawing in the black notebook that very night, under the date 18 December. Under the drawing he wrote a sentence, in his neatest handwriting: "Today I defended a thesis I didn't believe in and I won. Nevertheless, the person I learned the most from is the one I beat. Therefore, I think the best debate is the one in which, at the end, neither of the two needs to win any more." He reread it and thought it was a bit too serious for a thirteen-year-old. Then he added, underneath, in small letters: "P.S. The cup is crooked. Davide says it's a sign."
